# Hodgkin lymphoma

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > White blood cell and bone marrow disorders > Hodgkin lymphoma*

[Original Article Link](/library/mT0Vr2)

---

## Summary

Hodgkin <u>lymphoma</u> (HL) is a malignant <u>lymphoma</u> of <u>B-cell</u> origin. <u>Incidence</u> follows a bimodal age distribution, with peaks in the third, and sixth to eighth decades of life. The WHO classifies HL as either <u>classical HL</u> (<u>CHL</u>) or <u>nodular lymphocyte predominant HL</u> (<u>NLPHL</u>). Most patients (95%) with HL have <u>CHL</u>, which includes four histological subtypes: <u>nodular sclerosing CHL</u> (most common), mixed cellularity <u>CHL</u>, <u>lymphocyte-rich CHL</u>, and <u>lymphocyte-depleted CHL</u>. <u>Risk factors</u> for HL include <u>Epstein-Barr virus</u> (<u>EBV</u>) infection and <u>immunodeficiency</u> (e.g., due to <u>HIV infection</u>). <u>Clinical features of HL</u> include painless <u>lymphadenopathy</u>, <u>hepatosplenomegaly</u>, and <u>B symptoms</u>. <u>Pel-Ebstein fevers</u> and <u>alcohol-induced pain</u> in affected <u>lymph nodes</u> are rare but specific features of HL. <u>Excisional biopsy</u> of an affected <u>lymph node</u> or extranodal site is required to confirm the diagnosis; <u>Hodgkin cells</u> and <u>Reed-Sternberg cells</u> are present in <u>CHL</u> and <u>popcorn cells</u> are present in <u>NLPHL</u>. Staging is performed using the <u>Lugano classification</u>, which incorporates <u>histopathology</u> results, the presence of <u>B symptoms</u>, and <u>PET-CT scan</u> findings. Additional prognostic factors are used for risk <u>stratification</u> to guide treatment. Typically, <u>limited-stage HL</u> is treated with <u>chemotherapy</u> and <u>radiation therapy</u>, while <u>advanced-stage HL</u> is treated with <u>chemotherapy</u> alone. Overall, the prognosis is good with treatment. Patients require <u>ongoing management for HL</u> to monitor for disease recurrence and treatment-related complications (e.g., <u>second cancers</u>, cardiovascular disorders).

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Incidence</u>

* 2–3/100 000 per year [[1]](/library/Qn0uGg)

* Subtype <u>variance</u> with age (see “Pathology” below)

* Young adults: nodular <u>sclerosing</u> HL

* Elderly adults: mixed-cellularity HL

* Age: <u>bimodal distribution</u> [[2]](/library/HeXKZx)

* 1<sup>st</sup> peak: 25–30 years

* 2<sup>nd</sup> peak: 50–70 years

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[2]](/library/HeXKZx)

* Male predominance, especially in pediatric cases

* Exception: <u>♀</u> = <u>♂</u> in nodular <u>sclerosing</u> HL (most common type)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

The exact causes are unknown, but several <u>risk factors</u> have been associated with HL. [[3]](/library/kn0mtg)[[4]](/library/GeXBZx)




* Strong association with <u>Epstein-Barr virus</u> (<u>EBV</u>)

* <u>Immunodeficiency</u>: e.g., organ or cell <u>transplantation</u>, <u>immunosuppressants</u>, <u>HIV infection</u> , <u>chemotherapy</u>

* Autoimmune diseases (e.g., <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>)

---

## Clinical features

* Painless <u>lymphadenopathy</u>:

* First develops in a single group of <u>lymph nodes</u>; : typically cervical; , supraclavicular, or <u>mediastinal lymph nodes</u>  [[5]](/library/R0WlfP0)[[6]](/library/Cc1qef0)[[7]](/library/dxWovn0)

* Spreads contiguously through <u>the lymphatic system</u>: cervical nodes → <u>supraclavicular lymph nodes</u> → axillary nodes → <u>inguinal nodes</u>  [[8]](/library/QEWuvM0)

* <u>Splenomegaly</u> or <u>hepatomegaly</u>  [[9]](/library/Lwawj5)

* B symptoms [[10]](/library/teXX0x)

* Night sweats, weight loss > 10% in the past 6 months, <u>fever</u> > 38.0Â°C (> 100.4Â°F)

* Can occur in a variety of diseases (see “Differential diagnosis of <u>B symptoms</u>” below)

* In the case of confirmed HL, the presence of a single <u>B symptom</u> suffices for a positive diagnosis of <u>B symptoms</u>.

* Pel-Ebstein fever: <u>intermittent fever</u> with periods of high temperature for 1–2 weeks, followed by afebrile periods for 1–2 weeks; relatively rare but very specific for HL

* Alcohol-induced pain: <u>pain</u> in involved <u>lymph nodes</u> after ingestion of <u>alcohol</u>; relatively rare but highly specific for HL

* <u>Pruritus</u>: focal or generalized

## Diagnosis

* <u>Biopsy</u> is required to confirm the <u>diagnosis of HL</u> in patients with unexplained <u>lymphadenopathy</u> with or without <u>B symptoms</u>.

* Once the diagnosis is confirmed, further studies, including <u>PET-CT</u>, are required for <u>staging of HL</u>.





### Initial studies




<u>Laboratory studies</u> and imaging are not required for diagnosis but are commonly performed for the evaluation of <u>lymphadenopathy</u> and <u>B symptoms</u>.




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




* <u>CBC with differential</u> [[6]](/library/Cc1qef0)

* Elevated or decreased <u>WBC count</u>  [[11]](/library/cd1aKf0)

* <u>Anemia</u>

* <u>Eosinophilia</u>

* <u>Thrombocytosis</u> or <u>thrombocytopenia</u>

* <u>CMP</u> 

* <u>Elevated transaminases</u> and/or <u>hyperbilirubinemia</u>  [[12]](/library/FVXgwC)[[13]](/library/F6Xg5_)

* Elevated <u>alkaline phosphatase</u>  [[12]](/library/FVXgwC)

* <u>Hypoalbuminemia</u>  [[11]](/library/cd1aKf0)

* <u>Hypercalcemia</u> (uncommon) due to paraneoplastic production of <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u> [[12]](/library/FVXgwC)[[14]](/library/zc1rUf0)

* <u>ESR</u>: elevated  [[6]](/library/Cc1qef0)[[12]](/library/FVXgwC)

* <u>LDH</u>: elevated  [[12]](/library/FVXgwC)





#### Imaging




* <u>Ultrasound</u> or <u>CT scan</u>: Consider in individuals with palpable <u>lymphadenopathy</u> and/or <u>hepatosplenomegaly</u>.

* <u>CXR</u>: Consider in individuals with <u>generalized lymphadenopathy</u> to evaluate for <u>mediastinal</u> <u>lymphadenopathy</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Anemia</u>, <u>leukocytosis</u>, <u>leukopenia</u>, elevated <u>ESR</u>, elevated <u>LDH</u>, and <u>hypoalbuminemia</u> are all poor prognostic factors.




### Confirmatory <u>biopsy</u> [[6]](/library/Cc1qef0)[[8]](/library/QEWuvM0)[[15]](/library/K11U3f0)




* Modalities

* <u>Gold standard</u>: <u>excisional biopsy</u> of an involved <u>lymph node</u> or extranodal site

* Alternative: <u>core needle biopsy</u>

* Findings

* <u>Hodgkin cells</u> and <u>Reed-Sternberg cells</u>: <u>CHL</u>

* <u>Popcorn cells</u>: <u>NLPHL</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Excisional biopsy</u> is the <u>gold standard</u> for diagnosing HL. [[8]](/library/QEWuvM0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Fine-needle aspiration</u> is not recommended for suspected HL, as it cannot obtain sufficient tissue. [[6]](/library/Cc1qef0)[[12]](/library/FVXgwC)

## Differential diagnoses

### Differential diagnoses of B symptoms




* <u>Non-Hodgkin lymphomas</u>, Hodgkin <u>lymphomas</u>

* Other <u>hematopoietic</u> malignancies (e.g., <u>CML</u>, <u>ALL</u>)

* Solid tumors

* <u>Tuberculosis</u>

* <u>HIV</u>





### <u>Hodgkin vs. non-Hodgkin lymphoma</u>




| Hodgkin lymphoma vs. non-Hodgkin lymphoma |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feature | Hodgkin <u>lymphoma</u> | <u>Non-Hodgkin lymphoma</u> |
| Age distribution | <br>* Bimodal (late <u>adolescence</u> and older adulthood)<br><br> | <br>* Increases with age (peak > 50 years)<br><br> |
| Etiology | <br><br>* <u>Immunosuppression</u> (e.g., <u>HIV</u>)<br><br>* <u>EBV infection</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Chromosomal translocation</u>, commonly t(14;18)<br><br>* Autoimmune diseases (e.g., <u>Hashimoto thyroiditis</u>, rheumatic disease)<br><br>* Infections (<u>HIV</u>, <u>EBV</u>, <u>HTLV</u>-1)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Lymph node</u> involvement | <br><br>* <u>Lymph node groups</u> localized above the <u>diaphragm</u><br><br>* Contiguous spread<br><br>* Extranodal involvement rare<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Multiple <u>lymph node groups</u><br><br>* Noncontiguous spread<br><br>* Extranodal involvement common<br><br><br> |
| <u>Histology</u> | <br>* <u>Reed-Sternberg cells</u><br><br> | <br>* Majority are <u>neoplastic</u> cells of <u>B-cell</u> lineage<br><br> |
| Five-year survival rate | <br>* 80–90%<br><br> | <br>* ∼ 70%<br><br> |





### Other differential diagnoses




* “<u>Differential diagnoses of lymphadenopathy</u>”

* “<u>Differential diagnoses of granulomatous disease</u>”





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

## Pathology

* Reed-Sternberg cells (RSCs)

* <u>Tumor</u> cells that are <u>pathognomonic</u> of HL

* Originate from <u>B cells</u>

* Large cells with binuclear/bilobed <u>nuclei</u> with dark centers of <u>chromatin</u> and pale halos, which result in an owl-eye appearance on histopathologic examination.

* CD15/CD30-positive

* Hodgkin cells: mononuclear, malignant <u>B lymphocytes</u>

* Inflammatory background containing the following cell types in varying numbers: <u>lymphocytes</u>, <u>neutrophils</u>, <u>eosinophils</u>, <u>macrophages</u>/<u>histiocytes</u>, <u>plasma cells</u>, and <u>fibroblasts</u>

* <u>Granuloma</u> formation

| Histological <u>classification of Hodgkin lymphoma</u> (WHO) |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Classification | Subtype | Characteristics | Prognosis | Pathology |
| <br>Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (95%) | <br>Nodular sclerosing classical HL (<u>NSHL</u>) <br> | <br><br>* Most common subtype (> 60%)<br><br>* Localization: mostly <u>mediastinal</u> and cervical<br><br><br> | <br>* Good<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Nodules</u> of <u>Reed-Sternberg cells</u> within lacunae, separated by collagenous tissue with <u>sclerosing</u> appearance (hence the name “nodular <u>sclerosing</u>”).<br><br>* <u>Lymphocyte</u> rich.<br><br><br> |
| Mixed-cellularity classical HL (<u>MCHL</u>) | <br><br>* Commonly found in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients (e.g., <u>HIV</u>-positive individuals)<br><br>* Localization: mostly abdominal and splenic<br><br><br> | <br>* Good (but slightly worse than <u>NSHL</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Nodules</u> with numerous <u>Reed-Sternberg cells</u>, and increased number of <u>histiocytes</u>, <u>eosinophils</u>, and <u>plasma cells</u> (hence the name “mixed-cellularity”).<br><br> |  |
| Lymphocyte-rich classical HL (<u>LRHL</u>) | <br><br>* Rare<br><br>* Localization: mostly cervical and axillary<br><br><br> | <br>* Very good<br><br> | <br>* Presence of <u>Reed-Sternberg cells</u>, and reactive <u>lymphocytosis</u> that causes distortion of the <u>lymph node</u> architecture.<br><br> |  |
| Lymphocyte-depleted classical HL (<u>LDHL</u>) | <br><br>* Very rare (< 1%)<br><br>* Commonly found in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients<br><br>* Localization: mostly below the <u>diaphragm</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Poor<br><br> | <br>* Numerous <u>Reed-Sternberg cells</u>, and decreased number of <u>lymphocytes</u>.<br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Lymphocyte</u> predominant Hodgkin <u>lymphoma</u> (5%) | Nodular lymphocyte predominant HL (<u>NLPHL</u>) | <br><br>* Rare (5%)<br><br>* Localization: mostly neck, axillary, and inguinal [[16]](/library/AJXR9_)<br><br><br> | <br>* Very good (but slightly worse than <u>LRHL</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Presence of popcorn cells: a variant of a <u>Reed-Sternberg cell</u> characterized by polylobulated <u>nuclei</u> that resemble popcorn.<br><br>* <u>Lymphocyte</u> predominant (<u>LP</u>) cells express <u>CD20</u>, CD79a, and <u>CD45</u>. [[17]](/library/gmXFUA)<br><br>* Unlike in <u>classical Hodgkin lymphoma</u>, <u>tumor</u> cells are negative for CD15 and CD30. [[17]](/library/gmXFUA)<br><br><br> |

## Staging

### Lugano classification of lymphomas [[9]](/library/Lwawj5)




* The <u>Lugano classification</u> is used for <u>staging of HL</u> and <u>staging of NHL</u>.

* Imaging with <u>PET-CT</u> or <u>CT scan</u> is required.   [[9]](/library/Lwawj5)[[18]](/library/wc1hef0)[[19]](/library/zvWrcn0)





| <br><u>Lugano classification of primarily nodal lymphomas</u> [[9]](/library/Lwawj5)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage |  | Features |
| Limited-stage lymphoma | I | <br>* Isolated involvement of either:<br><br>* 1 <u>lymph node area</u> (I)<br><br>* 1 extranodal focus  (IE)<br><br> |
| II | <br>* Confined to one side of the <u>diaphragm</u> with involvement of any of the following:<br><br>* ≥ 2 <u>lymph node areas</u> (II)<br><br>* ≥ 1 <u>lymph node area</u> with limited contiguous extranodal spread (IIE)<br><br> |  |
| II bulky |  | <br>* Features of II or IIE with a large single nodal mass on <u>CT scan</u>  [[9]](/library/Lwawj5)<br><br> |
| Advanced-stage lymphoma | III | <br>* Involvement of either of the following:<br><br>* <u>Lymph nodes</u> on both sides of the <u>diaphragm</u><br><br>* Supradiaphragmatic <u>lymph nodes</u> plus the <u>spleen</u> (IIIS)<br><br> |
| IV | <br>* Disseminated, noncontiguous spread into extralymphatic organs (e.g., <u>liver</u>, <u>lung</u>, <u>bone marrow</u>)<br><br> |  |
| <br>A and B modifiers are only used for HL   [[9]](/library/Lwawj5) A: absence of <u>B symptoms</u> B: <u>B symptoms</u> present<br> |  |  |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Staging of HL</u> is based on the number of affected nodes, the presence or absence of <u>B symptoms</u>, and whether or not the disease is present on both sides of the <u>diaphragm</u>.

> [!TIP]
> Individuals who have undergone <u>PET-CT</u> do not routinely require <u>bone marrow biopsy</u>. [[6]](/library/Cc1qef0)[[15]](/library/K11U3f0)[[20]](/library/NT1-IT0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Bone marrow biopsy</u> is only indicated for staging if <u>PET-CT scan</u> imaging is unavailable or if there is evidence of <u>bone marrow</u> infiltration, e.g., <u>CBC</u> with <u>pancytopenia</u>, and the <u>PET-CT scan</u> does not demonstrate <u>bone marrow</u> involvement. [[8]](/library/QEWuvM0)[[9]](/library/Lwawj5)

## Risk stratification

Following <u>Lugano classification</u>, patients are assessed for the presence or absence of prognostic factors to make risk-based treatment decisions. [[8]](/library/QEWuvM0)[[15]](/library/K11U3f0)[[21]](/library/ET18sT0)




### Unfavorable prognostic factors for limited-stage HL [[6]](/library/Cc1qef0)[[20]](/library/NT1-IT0)[[21]](/library/ET18sT0)




All patients with <u>limited-stage HL</u> are assessed for unfavorable prognostic factors.  [[8]](/library/QEWuvM0)[[15]](/library/K11U3f0)




* <u>Risk factors</u>

* High <u>ESR</u>  [[8]](/library/QEWuvM0)[[12]](/library/FVXgwC)

* High <u>LDH</u> [[22]](/library/QxWuwn0)

* <u>B symptoms</u>

* Involvement of > 3 <u>lymph node areas</u>

* ≥ 1 extranodal site

* Bulky disease

* Age ≥ 50 years

* Interpretation

* Limited-stage favorable HL: <u>Limited-stage HL</u> without unfavorable prognostic factors

* Limited-stage unfavorable HL: <u>Limited-stage HL</u> with unfavorable prognostic factors





### International prognostic score (IPS) for advanced-stage HL




All patients with <u>advanced-stage HL</u> (i.e., <u>Lugano classification</u> III or IV) are assessed with the international prognostic score to guide treatment. [[11]](/library/cd1aKf0)[[15]](/library/K11U3f0)[[21]](/library/ET18sT0)




* <u>Risk factors</u>: One point is given for each <u>risk factor</u>.

* <u>Hypoalbuminemia</u> (< 4 g/dL)

* <u>Hemoglobin</u> < 10.5 g/dL

* Male sex

* Age ≥ 45 years

* <u>Lugano classification</u> stage IV

* <u>WBC</u> â¥ 15,000/mmÂ³

* <u>Lymphopenia</u>: <u>lymphocyte</u> count < 8% or absolute <u>lymphocyte</u> count < 600/mmÂ³

* Interpretation: Scores are used to estimate the freedom from progression (FFP) and overall survival (OS) at 5 years. [[23]](/library/rCWftn0)[[21]](/library/ET18sT0)

* IPS score 0–1: FFP ≥ 77%, OS ≥ 89%

* IPS score 2–3: FFP ∼60–67%, OS ∼ 78-81%

* IPS score 4–7: FFP < 51%, OS ≤ 61%





> [!TIP]
> Newer prediction models, e.g., the Advanced-stage <u>cHL</u> International Prognostication Index (A-HIPI), may be more accurate than the IPS due to improvements in treatment options. [[23]](/library/rCWftn0)[[24]](/library/exWxvn0)

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[15]](/library/K11U3f0)[[18]](/library/wc1hef0)




The following is performed by, or in coordination with, the patient's oncology team.




* Select a risk-based treatment option. Treatment for <u>CHL</u> includes:  [[25]](/library/011e2f0)

* Limited-stage favorable HL: short courses of <u>chemotherapy</u> plus <u>radiation therapy</u>   [[15]](/library/K11U3f0)

* <u>Limited-stage unfavorable HL</u>: may be treated with longer courses of <u>chemotherapy</u> ± <u>radiation therapy</u> [[15]](/library/K11U3f0)[[26]](/library/NU1-WT0)

* <u>Advanced-stage HL</u>: longer courses of <u>chemotherapy</u> without <u>radiation therapy</u>   [[15]](/library/K11U3f0)[[21]](/library/ET18sT0)

* Perform a pretreatment evaluation.

* All patients: routine <u>preparation for cancer treatment</u>, including screening studies for <u>pregnancy</u> and underlying comorbidities

* <u>Doxorubicin</u> candidates: <u>ECHO</u>  [[15]](/library/K11U3f0)

* <u>Bleomycin</u> candidates: <u>pulmonary function testing</u> with <u>DLCO</u>  [[27]](/library/zU1rfT0)

* Splenic radiation candidates: additional <u>vaccinations</u> as part of <u>infection prevention for asplenia</u>  [[28]](/library/k21m3T0)[[29]](/library/-U1DfT0)

* Provide ongoing <u>supportive care</u>.

* After treatment, provide <u>long-term management for HL</u>.

* See “<u>Principles of cancer care</u>” for information on <u>multidisciplinary care</u>, common cancer-related symptoms, and treatment-related complications.





> [!TIP]
> HL treatment has high cure rates. For all stages of HL, the initial goal of treatment is remission. [[8]](/library/QEWuvM0)




### <u>Chemotherapy</u> [[15]](/library/K11U3f0)[[18]](/library/wc1hef0)[[20]](/library/NT1-IT0)




* First-line treatment for all patients is typically ABVD: <u>Adriamycin</u><sup>®</sup> (<u>doxorubicin</u>), <u>bleomycin</u>, <u>vinblastine</u>, and dacarbazine.  [[6]](/library/Cc1qef0)[[12]](/library/FVXgwC)[[15]](/library/K11U3f0)

* Alternative treatments (e.g., in advanced-stage or refractory HL)

* Stanford V: <u>doxorubicin</u>, <u>vinblastine</u>, mechlorethamine, <u>vincristine</u>, <u>bleomycin</u>, <u>etoposide</u>, and <u>prednisone</u>

* BEACOPP: <u>bleomycin</u>, <u>etoposide</u>, <u>Adriamycin</u> (<u>doxorubicin</u>), <u>cyclophosphamide</u>, <u>Oncovin<sup>®</sup></u> (<u>vincristine</u>), <u>procarbazine</u>, and <u>prednisone</u>





### <u>Radiation therapy</u> [[20]](/library/NT1-IT0)[[25]](/library/011e2f0)




* Indication: patients with <u>limited-stage HL</u>, after <u>chemotherapy</u>  [[6]](/library/Cc1qef0)[[25]](/library/011e2f0)

* Radiation should target involved <u>lymph nodes</u> and/or extranodal sites.  [[6]](/library/Cc1qef0)





### Other treatments [[15]](/library/K11U3f0)[[20]](/library/NT1-IT0)[[25]](/library/011e2f0)




* <u>Autologous stem cell transplantation</u>: may be used after <u>high-dose chemotherapy</u> in patients with relapsed or refractory disease

* Immunotherapy (e.g., brentuximab, <u>nivolumab</u>, or <u>pembrolizumab</u>) may be used for:

* Initial treatment of advanced HL

* Prevention of relapse after <u>autologous stem cell transplantation</u>

* Management of relapsed or refractory disease

---

## Prognosis

* Overall, HL has a good prognosis with a 5-year survival rate of ∼ 80–90% (in children, > 95%). [[18]](/library/wc1hef0)[[20]](/library/NT1-IT0)[[36]](/library/3W1SOf0)

* <u>Lymphocyte-rich classical HL</u> (<u>LRHL</u>) and <u>nodular lymphocyte predominant HL</u> (<u>NLPHL</u>) have the best prognoses among HL subtypes.  [[37]](/library/DT11GT0)[[38]](/library/wT1hGT0)

* Prognosis is largely determined by disease stage.

* There is an increased risk for treatment-related <u>second malignancies</u> (e.g., <u>breast</u>, <u>lung</u>, colorectal).  [[39]](/library/bd1Hof0)
